item.question: A 5 × 3 grid (5 rows, 3 columns) has its top right square removed. Can the remaining 14 squares be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
steps_tex: $14$ squares would need $7$ tiles.
Top row: the two squares left form one horizontal tile.
Rows $2$ and $3$: put a vertical tile in each of the $3$ columns.
Rows $4$ and $5$: put a vertical tile in each of the $3$ columns.
That is $1 + 3 + 3 = 7$ tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.
item.answer_tex: Yes: $1$ horizontal tile in the top row and $6$ vertical tiles below

item.question: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its second row removed. Can the remaining squares be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
steps_tex: $14$ squares would need $7$ tiles.
Row $1$: the left two squares form one horizontal tile.
The top right square goes with the square below it: one vertical tile.
The left square of row $2$ goes with the left square of row $3$: one vertical tile.
The middle and right squares of row $3$ form one horizontal tile.
Rows $4$ and $5$: one vertical tile in each of the $3$ columns.
That is $4$ tiles above and $3$ tiles below, $7$ tiles with no gaps and no overlaps.
item.answer_tex: Yes: a tiling with $7$ tiles exists

item.question: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its top row removed. Colour it like a chessboard with white corners, and decide whether it can be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
steps_tex: With white corners, the full $5 \times 3$ grid has $8$ white and $7$ black squares.
The top middle square sits between two white corners, so it is black.
After removing it, $8$ white and $6$ black squares are left.
Each $2 \times 1$ tile covers two neighbouring squares, and neighbours have different colours, so each tile covers one white and one black.
$7$ tiles would cover $7$ white and $7$ black squares, but there are $8$ white and $6$ black.
So no tiling exists.
item.answer_tex: Not tileable: $8$ white and $6$ black squares remain, but every tile covers one of each

item.question: Use the colouring to find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable.
steps_tex: Colour the $5 \times 3$ grid with white corners: $8$ white and $7$ black squares.
Removing any black square leaves $8$ white and $6$ black, which no set of tiles can cover.
The black squares are the ones whose row number plus column number is odd.
Besides the top middle square, these are: row $2$, column $1$; row $2$, column $3$; row $3$, column $2$; row $4$, column $1$; row $4$, column $3$; row $5$, column $2$.
For example, removing the square in row $2$, column $1$ makes the grid non-tileable.
item.answer_tex: Any black square works, for example row $2$, column $1$; the others are row $2$ column $3$, row $3$ column $2$, row $4$ column $1$, row $4$ column $3$ and row $5$ column $2$

item.question: Is the following tiling possible? Region to be tiled: 12 unit squares in 4 rows, where the top two rows have 2 squares each, at the left, and the bottom two rows have 4 squares each. Tile: an L shape of 3 unit squares (two squares stacked, with one more square beside the bottom one). The tile may be turned.
steps_tex: $12$ squares need $4$ tiles of $3$ squares.
One way: cover the top left square with an $L$ that also covers the square beside it and the square below it, in rows $1$ and $2$.
Then row $2$, column $2$ is left in the top part; cover it with row $3$, columns $2$ and $3$, in an $L$.
Row $3$, column $1$ goes with row $4$, columns $1$ and $2$, in an $L$.
Row $3$, column $4$ goes with row $4$, columns $3$ and $4$, in an $L$.
All $12$ squares are covered by $4$ tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.

item.question: Is the following tiling possible? Region to be tiled: an 8 × 8 grid with the top right corner square and the bottom left corner square removed. Tile: 2 × 1.
steps_tex: The region has $64$ squares minus $2$, which is $62$ squares, an even number.
Colour it like a chessboard. In an $8 \times 8$ board, the top right and bottom left corners have the same colour, say black.
The full board has $32$ white and $32$ black squares. Removing two black ones leaves $32$ white and $30$ black.
Each $2 \times 1$ tile covers one white and one black square.
$31$ tiles would cover $31$ of each colour, but the counts are $32$ and $30$.
So the region cannot be tiled.
item.answer_tex: Not possible: the two removed corners have the same colour, leaving $32$ of one colour and $30$ of the other

concept_name: Squares, triangles and hexagons tile the plane

item.question: Explain why squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons can each tile the whole plane.
steps: Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must fill the full 360° with no gap and no overlap.
A square has angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360, so four squares fill a corner.
An equilateral triangle has angles of 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360, so six triangles fill a corner.
A regular hexagon has angles of 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360, so three hexagons fill a corner.
Repeating these corners in every direction covers the whole plane.
item.answer: Each angle goes into 360° exactly: four 90°, six 60°, three 120°
item.text:
Worked example: Explain why squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons can each tile the whole plane.
1. Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must fill the full 360° with no gap and no overlap.
2. A square has angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360, so four squares fill a corner.
3. An equilateral triangle has angles of 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360, so six triangles fill a corner.
4. A regular hexagon has angles of 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360, so three hexagons fill a corner.
5. Repeating these corners in every direction covers the whole plane.
Answer: Each angle goes into 360° exactly: four 90°, six 60°, three 120°
